findings.title: Docstring describes old return type
findings.body:
The docstring states 'Return (name, email) for a user.' but the function now returns a dictionary with keys 'name', 'email', and 'tier'. A caller reading the docstring will expect a tuple and will unpack it incorrectly, causing an immediate runtime error. Update the docstring to match the new return shape.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Docstring still documents the removed (name, email) tuple contract

findings.title: Return shape changed from tuple to dict, breaking unpacking callers
findings.body: `lookup_user` previously returned a 2-tuple `(name, email)`; it now returns a dict with three keys. Any existing caller written as `name, email = lookup_user(id)` will now unpack the dict's *keys*, and because there are three of them it raises `ValueError: too many values to unpack (expected 2)` at runtime — a hard failure, not a silent wrong value. Either update every call site in the same change, or keep backward compatibility (e.g. return a `NamedTuple` with `name`/`email`/`tier` fields, which unpacks as a 2-... no — a 3-field NamedTuple still breaks 2-target unpacking, so the call sites must be updated either way). Grep for `lookup_user(` and fix each caller.

Without such a test, the breaking change can ship silently.

findings.title: Removed None guard crashes on invoices without a purchase order
findings.body:
The previous code only appended the PO line when `invoice.purchase_order is not None`; the rewritten literal calls `.upper()` unconditionally. For any invoice where `purchase_order` is `None` — which the removed guard shows is a real, expected state — this raises `AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'upper'` and the whole render fails.

There is a second, quieter consequence: the return shape changed from a 1-or-2 element list to an always-2-element list, so any caller that indexes or measures the result (e.g. treating `len(lines) == 2` as "this invoice has a PO") now sees a literal `PO None` line instead.

Keep the conditional, e.g. build the base list and append the PO line only when `invoice.purchase_order` is set.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Dropped None guard makes header_lines raise on optional PO field

_Also raised by the docs agent:_ Public function now assumes non-null field without documenting it

findings.title: No test covers invoice with missing purchase_order
findings.body: The removed guard `if invoice.purchase_order is not None` handled the case where purchase_order is None; now `invoice.purchase_order.upper()` is called unconditionally, which will raise AttributeError for invoices without a PO. No test in this diff exercises header_lines with a None purchase_order, so this regression would not be caught by any existing or added test.

findings.title: Retry wraps a non-idempotent charge, risking duplicate charges
findings.body:
`charge(card_token, amount_cents)` is a state-mutating payment operation. `@retry(attempts=3)` will re-invoke it on any failure the decorator considers retryable, including a network timeout or 5xx that occurs *after* the gateway has already accepted and captured the charge. The result is up to three real charges against the customer's card for one logical request.

The read wrapper directly above (`fetch_charge` -> `get_charge`) is safe precisely because it is idempotent; the same decorator is not transferable to the write path.

Fixes, in rough order of preference:
- Pass a caller-supplied idempotency key through to `charge(...)` so the gateway collapses retried attempts into one charge, and only then retry.
- If the gateway has no idempotency support, drop the retry here and surface the failure, or retry only on errors that provably occurred before submission (e.g. connection-refused / DNS), never on timeouts or 5xx.

findings.title: Public charge function lacks idempotency contract documentation
findings.body: The `charge_card` function wraps a payment operation with retry logic, but provides no documentation about idempotency guarantees or the consequences of retries. A caller who does not know whether `charge(card_token, amount_cents)` is idempotent could unknowingly trigger duplicate charges if the function retries. This is a critical contract gap for a financial operation.

findings.title: No test covers retry-on-failure behavior for charge_card
findings.body: charge_card wraps a non-idempotent payment call with @retry(attempts=3). There is no test in this diff verifying what happens when the underlying charge() call fails transiently and is retried — specifically whether retries could cause duplicate charges. Since this operation moves money, a test exercising failure/retry semantics (e.g. mocking charge() to fail once then succeed, and asserting it isn't invoked more times than intended, or that idempotency is enforced) would catch a regression where retry logic causes a double charge.

findings.title: Naive datetime.now() subtracted from aware expires_at raises TypeError
findings.body:
`cutoff` is built with `datetime.now()` (no tzinfo), but `invite.expires_at` is timezone-aware — line 5 compares it directly against `datetime.now(timezone.utc)`, which only succeeds for aware values. Python raises `TypeError: can't subtract offset-naive and offset-aware datetimes` for the subtraction on line 10, so every call to `expires_within` fails. Use `datetime.now(timezone.utc)` for the cutoff, matching `is_expired`. (Even if `expires_at` were naive, `datetime.now()` returns local time while line 5 assumes UTC, so the two functions would disagree by the UTC offset.)

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Naive cutoff in expires_within skews or breaks expiry enforcement

_Also raised by the docs agent:_ Public function `expires_within` lacks docstring

findings.title: expires_within has no test; naive/aware bug would go undetected

This raises TypeError at runtime when expires_at is timezone-aware. findings.title: Public function `contactEmail` undocumented; contract with optional `Account` unclear
findings.body:
The exported function `contactEmail` accepts an `Account` parameter. Callers have no way to know from the signature or documentation whether `account.billingContact` or `account.billingContact.email` may be null or undefined. The implementation accesses `.email` without optional chaining, which means the function will throw at runtime if `billingContact` or `email` are missing — but this is not documented. A caller passing an account without a billing contact, or without an email in the contact, will get a cryptic TypeError rather than the documented contract of the function. Either the function must document that it throws when those fields are absent, or must defensively handle them as the sibling function `bannerFor` does on line 4.

findings.title: Lowering retries default from 5 to 1 silently changes caller behaviour
findings.body:
`fetch` previously retried up to 5 times by default; it now retries once. Every existing call site that omits `retries` gets a 5x reduction in resilience without any code change on their side, and the failure mode is intermittent (transient upstream errors that used to be absorbed now surface as exceptions/failed responses), so it will not be caught by a build and may only show up as elevated error rates in production.

If the intent is to stop over-retrying at a specific call site, pass `retries=1` explicitly there and leave the default alone. If the default genuinely must change, audit the call sites that rely on it and pin the ones fronting known-flaky dependencies to their previous value in the same change.

Secondary point worth confirming while you are here: `_with_retries` was not shown, so it is unclear whether `retries=1` means "one attempt total" or "one initial attempt plus one retry". At the old value of 5 the off-by-one was immaterial; at 1 it is the difference between retrying and not retrying at all.

findings.body: The default for `retries` was lowered from 5 to 1, which changes behavior for any caller relying on the implicit default (e.g. a known flaky dependency mentioned in the PR description). No test exists to verify that `fetch()` called without an explicit `retries` argument still succeeds against a flaky/retrying dependency, so this regression would not be caught by any test suite.

findings.title: Index name suffix `idx2` suggests a duplicate of an existing index
findings.body:
This creates a second index on `invoices (tenant_id, created_at DESC)` under a name that differs from the conventional `invoices_tenant_created_idx` only by a trailing `2`. That naming pattern is what you get when the intended name is already taken — i.e. an equivalent index on the same table and the same leading columns already exists from an earlier migration. If so, this index buys no read benefit and permanently costs a write amplification plus its own storage and vacuum load on what is presumably a high-volume `invoices` table.

Before merging, grep the earlier migrations for `ON invoices (tenant_id` and check `pg_indexes` on a production-like database. If an equivalent index exists, drop this statement; if the existing one differs in a way that matters (e.g. ASC vs DESC, or a partial predicate), rename this one to something descriptive so the distinction is recorded rather than encoded as a counter.

findings.title: CREATE INDEX without CONCURRENTLY takes an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock
findings.body:
A plain `CREATE INDEX` holds an `ACCESS EXCLUSIVE`-blocking `SHARE` lock on `invoices` for the duration of the build, blocking all writes (inserts, updates, deletes) to the table until it completes. On a table large enough to warrant a composite `(tenant_id, created_at DESC)` index, that is a write outage for the length of the build.

Use `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY`, noting that it cannot run inside a transaction block — so the migration runner must be configured to execute this statement outside its usual wrapping transaction, and the migration should be checked for a left-behind `INVALID` index on failure.

findings.title: Referer header logged unscrubbed, leaking auth tokens into logs
findings.body:
The removed branch passed the `Referer` value through `_scrub_uri(value, extra_param_keys)` before adding it to the logged header dict; the replacement copies `request.headers[header]` for every header, including `Referer`, straight into `headers` which is then serialised by `log_method(json.dumps(headers, indent=2))` on line 6.

Jupyter Server authenticates via a `?token=...` query parameter. When a user opens a notebook URL containing the token, the browser sends that full URL as `Referer` on subsequent requests, so the token is written in cleartext to the server log. Anyone who can read the log file, a log shipper, or an ops dashboard then holds a working credential for that server — this is exactly what the `_scrub_uri` call existed to prevent (`extra_param_keys` is the list of sensitive query keys to redact).

Restore the per-header handling so `Referer` (and any other URI-bearing header) is passed through `_scrub_uri` before being stored.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Referer is logged unscrubbed, re-exposing tokens in logs

findings.body: The change removes the call to _scrub_uri for the Referer header, meaning any token embedded in the Referer query string would now be logged verbatim. If a test previously existed asserting that a token-bearing Referer is scrubbed before logging, it either doesn't exist or wasn't run/updated here — nothing in this diff's context shows a test catching this regression. Since no test file is part of this PR, this behavior change would go undetected.

findings.title: xlinkhref no longer validated, reintroducing javascript: URI XSS
findings.body:
`xlinkhref` was dropped from the condition that dispatches to `isAnchorLinkAllowed(value)`. With it removed, an `xlink:href` attribute in untrusted markdown falls through to whatever the default branch does (presumably 'allowed'), so `<svg><a xlink:href="javascript:...">` is emitted verbatim into the DOM. SVG `xlink:href` is script-executable in the same way `href` is, which is exactly why it was grouped with `href` and `src` here. Unless the value is scheme-checked elsewhere on this path — nothing in the diff suggests it is — restore `|| attribute === 'xlinkhref'` to the condition.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ xlink:href no longer scheme-checked, re-enabling SVG-based XSS

findings.title: No test guards xlinkhref sanitisation removal
findings.body: The change removes the 'xlinkhref' check from the sanitiser condition, reintroducing an XSS vector via SVG xlink:href attributes in untrusted markdown. No test file is part of this diff, and no existing test is shown that exercises isAnchorLinkAllowed with an 'xlinkhref' attribute. If such a test existed and was strong, this change should have failed CI; since it's presented as a straightforward regression, it's likely no test asserts that 'xlinkhref' attributes are sanitised the same way as 'href'/'src'.

findings.title: Project query parameter reaches downstream unvalidated (path traversal)
findings.body:
`projectQueryParameter` comes straight from the request query string and, after this change, no longer passes through `common.ValidateID` before being used. The only remaining guard is the equality check on line 4, which is skipped entirely when `parameters.Project` is empty — i.e. for the non-project-scoped list route the value flows downstream completely unchecked. Where the value is used as a filesystem path component, inputs such as `../../etc` or an absolute path escape the intended directory; where it is used in a store lookup it violates the identifier contract every downstream consumer was written against.

Restore the `common.ValidateID(projectQueryParameter)` check (returning `HandleBadRequestError`) before any use of the value. If the intent was to relax the rule for a specific caller, the relaxation belongs at that caller, not by deleting the shared guard.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Project query parameter reaches storage path without ValidateID check

findings.title: No test guards against removal of project ID validation
findings.body: The removed call to common.ValidateID(projectQueryParameter) enforced that the project query parameter is a well-formed identifier before being used downstream (likely as part of a filesystem path). No test in this diff exercises list() with a malformed/path-traversal-like projectQueryParameter to confirm it is rejected. If such a test existed prior to this change, it apparently did not fail, or it was not included in this diff; either way nothing here would catch a reintroduction of the invalid-path bug this validation was meant to prevent.

findings.title: DELETE now authorized as "push"; the "delete" action is never produced
findings.body:
The previous switch produced four distinct actions (`pull`, `push`, `delete`, and a `pull` default). The new expression can only ever yield `pull` or `push`, so `http.MethodDelete` falls into the `!= GET && != HEAD` branch and is authorized as `push`.

Consequence: any principal (or token scope) granted push on a repository can now delete tags/manifests/blobs, and any policy rule or token scope written against the `delete` action becomes dead — it will never match a request, so delete-specific grants stop working and delete-specific denies stop protecting anything. This is exactly the inversion of the fix that separated DELETE from push.

Restore the explicit `case http.MethodDelete: action = "delete"` branch (the collapse is only safe for the push methods POST/PATCH/PUT).

_Also raised by the security agent:_ DELETE now requires only push access, re-enabling privilege escalation

findings.title: Default for unlisted methods flipped from "pull" to "push"
findings.body:
The removed `default: action = "pull"` arm meant any method outside the enumerated set (OPTIONS, TRACE, CONNECT, or a non-standard verb) was treated as a read. The new condition classifies every such method as `push`, so a client that previously only needed pull access now needs push and will receive a 401/403 instead.

If the broadened default is intentional (fail-closed), it deserves an explicit comment; if not, keep the method set explicit and default unknown verbs to `pull` as before.

findings.title: No test guards DELETE→action mapping after collapsing cases
findings.body: The change collapses the method-to-action switch so that http.MethodDelete now falls into the generic push branch instead of its own "delete" action. This is a behavioural change to the authorization action assigned to DELETE requests. No test in this diff exercises a DELETE request and asserts the resulting ResourceAction.Action value, so nothing would fail if this mapping is wrong (e.g. if delete should require a distinct "delete" permission rather than "push").

findings.title: Public `location` attribute changes from str to URL
findings.body:
Previously `self.location` retained exactly the value passed in by the caller (typically a `str`); it is now replaced by `URL(location)`. Any existing consumer that treats the attribute as a string — `exc.location.startswith('/')`, `exc.location == '/login'`, `'%s' % exc.location` in a comparison, JSON serialisation of the attribute, or `isinstance(..., str)` checks — silently changes behaviour: equality against a string returns `False` rather than raising, so failures are quiet rather than loud. Note also that `URL()` normalises/encodes, so even `str(self.location)` may not round-trip the original input.

If the URL object is genuinely wanted, keep the original string available (e.g. compute `url = URL(location)` locally for the header and leave `self.location = location`), or make the type change deliberate with a changelog entry and a documented deprecation for str-consumers.

_Also raised by the docs agent:_ Public attribute type changed without visible documentation update

findings.title: No test verifies self.location's type after this change
findings.body: self.location now stores a URL object rather than the original string/URL argument passed in. This is a public attribute whose type contract just changed (again, per the PR description reverting a prior fix). No test in this diff asserts what type or value self.location holds after construction, so a regression here (e.g. reverting the assignment order or type again) would not be caught.

findings.title: readany can return empty bytes before EOF after while→if change
findings.body:
`_wait('readany')` returning does not guarantee that `self._buffer` is now non-empty. The waiter future is resolved by any of the wake-up paths (e.g. `feed_data` with a zero-length payload, `feed_eof`, `set_exception`, or a cancellation/timeout-adjacent wake), so control can reach `self._read_nowait(-1)` with an empty buffer and no EOF set. `_read_nowait(-1)` then returns `b''`.

That breaks the documented contract of `readany`: it must return a non-empty chunk unless the stream is at EOF. Every consumer that loops `while True: chunk = await content.readany(); if not chunk: break` — including `__aiter__`/`iter_any` style iteration — will silently treat the empty result as end-of-stream and truncate the response body. No exception is raised, so the failure is a silent short read.

Restore the loop so the wake-up condition is re-checked:

```python
while not self._buffer and not self._eof:
    await self._wait('readany')
```

The loop form is the standard guard against spurious wakeups and is what the original fix introduced; the `if` form is strictly weaker and only coincidentally correct when the wake always carries data.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Single `if` lets readany return empty bytes before EOF

findings.title: No test guards against spurious-wakeup regression in read()
findings.body: Changing the loop to a single if means that if `_wait('readany')` returns without the buffer being populated (a spurious wakeup), `read()` will return an empty/premature result instead of waiting again. No test in this diff exercises this scenario (e.g. simulating `_wait` resolving with an empty buffer still not at eof), so this regression would pass unnoticed through CI.

findings.title: Removing None guard reintroduces TypeError on missing/malformed cookies
findings.body: `if name in self.request.cookies:` raises `TypeError: argument of type 'NoneType' is not iterable` whenever `request.cookies` is `None`. The removed condition (`self.request.cookies is not None and ...`) existed precisely to handle that case — per the PR description it was the fix for a crash on a malformed `Cookie` header. With it gone, any request whose cookie parsing yields `None` turns a documented "return `default`" contract into an unhandled exception, i.e. a 500 for every handler that calls `get_cookie` (which includes `get_secure_cookie`/XSRF paths). Restore the `is not None` check, or ensure `request.cookies` is guaranteed to be a dict on every code path before relying on it here.

findings.title: Dropping None check on request.cookies allows remote 500 via Cookie header
findings.body:
`get_cookie` now evaluates `name in self.request.cookies` without first confirming `self.request.cookies` is not `None`. The entry point is the attacker-supplied `Cookie:` request header, which is parsed into `request.cookies`; the sink is the membership test on line 3. When parsing yields `None` (the malformed-header case the removed guard existed for, per the PR description), `name in None` raises `TypeError`, which surfaces as an unhandled 500.

This is reachable by any unauthenticated client on every handler that calls `get_cookie` — including the secure-cookie and XSRF paths that are typically invoked in `prepare`/`get_current_user` — so a single malformed header turns into a cheap, repeatable error-response generator and pollutes error logs with stack traces.

Restore the guard (`if self.request.cookies is not None and name in self.request.cookies:`) or, better, make the `cookies` property return an empty dict on parse failure so callers never see `None`.

findings.title: No test guards against request.cookies being None
findings.body: The diff removes the `self.request.cookies is not None` check, which per the PR description was added to fix a crash on a malformed Cookie header. There is no test in this diff exercising get_cookie with a malformed/missing Cookie header (where request.cookies could be None), so this regression would not be caught by CI.

findings.title: Missing ownership check lets any user edit another user's payment method
findings.body:
`update_payment_method` takes `pm_id` straight from the request routing, loads the object with `PaymentMethod.get(pm_id)`, and writes `body["billing_name"]` onto it before calling `pm.save()`. No authorisation check stands between the lookup and the mutation. The read handler directly above (line 6) calls `require_owner(current_user(request), pm)` on exactly the same object, so the control exists and is simply not applied on the write path — the stronger of the two operations. The `user = current_user(request)` on line 11 is computed and then never used, which reads like the check was intended and dropped.

Any authenticated caller can enumerate or guess `pm_id` values and rewrite the billing name on payment methods belonging to other accounts. Add the same guard immediately after the load:

    user = current_user(request)
    pm = PaymentMethod.get(pm_id)
    require_owner(user, pm)

Authentication alone (having a session) is not authorisation for *this* object.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ update_payment_method mutates object without require_owner check

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Unguarded body["billing_name"] raises KeyError on malformed input

findings.body: update_payment_method loads a PaymentMethod by id and mutates/saves it without calling require_owner (unlike the adjacent get handler at line 6). There is no test in this diff exercising this function, so a regression or an intentional authz bypass here would not be caught by any existing suite. At minimum a test should assert that a non-owner calling update_payment_method is rejected, and that an owner's update actually persists the new billing_name.

findings.title: Ownership enforcement removed from bulk_export (IDOR)
findings.body:
`bulk_export` previously called `require_owner(user, report)` for every requested report before serialising. That loop and the `require_owner` import were deleted, so the function now fetches whatever IDs the caller supplies and returns `r.to_dict()` for all of them with no access control. If the check is genuinely a performance problem, replace it with a bulk-scoped query (e.g. fetch reports filtered by owner in one call, and 403/404 on any requested ID not in the result) rather than dropping enforcement. Note that `user = current_user(request)` on line 5 is now unused, which is itself the signal that the only authorisation step is gone.

The `bulk_export` function now exports reports belonging to any user, not just the caller's own reports. This is a material change to the security boundary of a public API endpoint. findings.title: SQL injection via f-string interpolation in search_customers
findings.body:
`search_customers` builds its query with an f-string, splicing `term` and `status` straight into single-quoted SQL literals, then passes the finished string to `execute()` with no parameter tuple. A caller-supplied `status` of `x' OR '1'='1` returns every customer row; `x'; DROP TABLE customers; --` is available if the driver permits multiple statements, and `term` is equally exposed. Note that `execute` is called with a single argument here, so nothing downstream can re-bind these values.

Fix it the same way `get_customer` on line 5 already does — use placeholders and pass a parameter tuple, building the LIKE wildcards into the bound value rather than the SQL text:

```python
def search_customers(term, status):
    sql = "SELECT * FROM customers WHERE name LIKE %s AND status = %s"
    return execute(sql, (f"%{term}%", status))
```

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ search_customers interpolates term/status directly into SQL

findings.title: New search_customers function has no test coverage
findings.body: search_customers builds a SQL query via f-string interpolation of term and status with no tests included in this change. Nothing would catch a regression in this function's SQL construction or an injection-style input causing broken queries or unexpected results.

findings.title: Mock patches definition site, so real deliver() still runs
findings.body:
`test_send_gives_up_after_three_failures` patches `notify.transport.deliver`, but the sibling test one line above patches `notify.sender.deliver` — which only works if `notify.sender` did `from notify.transport import deliver`, binding its own module-level name. Patching the defining module rebinds `notify.transport.deliver` but leaves `notify.sender.deliver` pointing at the original function, so `send_with_retry` calls the real implementation: no mocked failures, possibly real I/O, and the assertion passes or fails for reasons unrelated to the retry logic.

Change the target to `notify.sender.deliver` to match line 2. To make the test actually prove the retry path, assert on call count as well (e.g. keep a handle on the mock and assert it was called three times), otherwise a `send_with_retry` that gives up after one attempt would still return `False` and pass.

_Also raised by the tests agent:_ Patch targets wrong module path, mock never used

findings.title: csv_rows joins raw values and never calls csv_escape
findings.body:
`csv_rows` joins `str(r.get(c, ""))` with commas directly. Any cell containing a comma, a double quote, or a newline is emitted unescaped, producing a line with the wrong field count that no CSV reader will parse back correctly. `csv_escape`, added immediately below in the same commit, is exactly the fix and is currently unreferenced (dead code) — the row builder should be `",".join(csv_escape(str(r.get(c, ""))) for c in columns)`.

Note also that `csv_escape` assumes a `str`: `"," in value` raises `TypeError` for an int, float or `None`. Wiring it in after the `str(...)` conversion in `csv_rows` avoids that, but any other caller passing a raw cell value will hit it.

findings.title: csv_rows joins fields unescaped, bypassing csv_escape
findings.body:
`csv_rows` renders each field with `str(r.get(c, ""))` and joins on `,`, never calling the `csv_escape` helper defined immediately below it. Any field value that contains a comma (or a quote, or a newline) will split into additional CSV fields, shifting every subsequent column for that row and letting whoever controls the field content forge column values in the exported file. If the row data originates from user-supplied records, this is field-delimiter injection into the export consumed downstream (spreadsheet import, billing pipeline, etc.).

Fix: apply the escaping on the way out, e.g. `",".join(csv_escape(str(r.get(c, ""))) for c in columns)`, and extend `csv_escape` to also quote values containing `\n`/`\r`. Using `csv.writer` from the stdlib would remove the whole class of bug. Separately, consider whether values beginning with `=`, `+`, `-` or `@` need neutralising for spreadsheet formula injection.

findings.title: New exporter functions added with no tests

findings.title: Retry wraps a non-idempotent charge with no idempotency key
findings.body:
`@retry(attempts=3)` on `charge_card` will re-invoke `charge(card_token, amount_cents)` on any failure the decorator considers retryable. Payment capture is not idempotent: if the gateway actually processed the charge but the response was lost (timeout, connection reset, 5xx after commit), the retry submits a second and possibly third capture for the same card and amount — the customer is charged 2–3x and the money has to be refunded manually.

The contrast with `fetch_charge` on lines 5–7 is the point: a read is safe to retry, a write that moves money is not. Fix by either (a) threading a caller-supplied idempotency key through to `charge(...)` so the gateway deduplicates replays, or (b) dropping the retry here and letting the caller decide, or (c) restricting the retry to errors that provably occurred before the request reached the gateway (e.g. connection-establishment failures only) rather than all exceptions.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Retry on non-idempotent charge can double-debit without idempotency key

findings.title: No test guards retry-on-charge against duplicate charges
findings.body: charge_card wraps a payment-charging call with @retry(attempts=3). If the underlying charge() call succeeds but the response is lost (a classic case for retries), retrying will submit the charge again, potentially billing the customer multiple times. There is no test in this diff verifying idempotency or that charge_card is not retried on ambiguous/partial failures, so a regression here (e.g. someone loosening the retry policy further, or the gateway remaining non-idempotent) would not be caught by any existing suite.

findings.title: Naive datetime.now() subtracted from aware expires_at raises TypeError
findings.body:
Line 9 creates `cutoff` from `datetime.now()`, which is timezone-naive. Line 5 in the same module compares `invite.expires_at` against `datetime.now(timezone.utc)`, which only succeeds if `expires_at` is timezone-aware. Subtracting a naive datetime from an aware one raises `TypeError: can't subtract offset-naive and offset-aware datetimes`, so `expires_within` fails for every invite, not just an edge case.

Use `cutoff = datetime.now(timezone.utc).replace(microsecond=0)` to match the convention already established by `is_expired`. Note that even if `expires_at` were naive, `datetime.now()` returns local wall-clock time, which would silently offset the result by the machine's UTC offset.

findings.title: CREATE INDEX without CONCURRENTLY blocks writes on `invoices`
findings.body:
`invoices` is not created by this migration — the `CREATE TABLE` above it defines a different, reporting-side table with `started_at`, not `created_at`. So this statement builds an index on an existing, presumably populated production table. A plain `CREATE INDEX` takes a `SHARE` lock, which blocks all `INSERT`/`UPDATE`/`DELETE` on `invoices` for the entire build. On a large invoices table that is a write outage for the duration.

Use `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY IF NOT EXISTS ...`, and make sure the migration runner executes this statement outside a transaction block — `CONCURRENTLY` cannot run inside one. Note that a concurrent build can leave an `INVALID` index behind if it fails, so the migration should be re-runnable, which `IF NOT EXISTS` alone does not guarantee.

findings.title: Index name suffix `idx2` suggests a duplicate of an existing index
findings.body:
The name `invoices_tenant_created_idx2` is the shape a name takes when `invoices_tenant_created_idx` already exists and the natural name collided. Postgres will happily create a second index with identical columns and ordering under a different name — it does not deduplicate — so if an earlier migration already created `invoices (tenant_id, created_at DESC)`, this doubles the write amplification and storage for that table with no read benefit, and leaves two indexes for future migrations to keep in sync.

Before merging, grep the earlier migrations for an index on `invoices (tenant_id, created_at)`. If one exists, drop this statement; if the existing one differs (e.g. ASC ordering, or an extra column), say so in the migration as a comment and give this index a name that describes why it is different rather than `idx2`.

findings.title: Referer header logged unscrubbed, leaking auth tokens into logs
findings.body:
The removed branch redacted sensitive query parameters from the `Referer` value via `_scrub_uri(value, extra_param_keys)` before it was placed into the `headers` dict that is serialised and written by `log_method`. After this change the raw header goes straight to the log sink.

Jupyter Server authenticates browser sessions via a `?token=<auth token>` query parameter in the URL. When a page loaded at such a URL issues a subsequent request, the browser sends that full URL — token included — as `Referer`. This handler runs on request logging (the PR title says on 5xx), so the session token is written verbatim into the server log, where it is readable by anyone with log access, log shipping/aggregation, or a support bundle. A token recovered this way grants full authenticated access to the notebook server, i.e. arbitrary code execution as the server user.

Restore the conditional scrub:

```python
value = request.headers[header]
if header == "Referer":
    value = _scrub_uri(value, extra_param_keys)
headers[header] = value
```

If `_scrub_uri` now has no other caller, keep it rather than deleting it.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Referer no longer scrubbed before being written to the log

findings.title: No test guards against unscrubbed Referer header in logs
findings.body: The change removes the call to _scrub_uri for the Referer header, restoring verbatim logging of what could be a token-bearing URL. No test file is part of this PR, and if a prior test existed asserting that logged Referer values are scrubbed (e.g., checking that a token/query param is absent from the log output), it would have failed here — but since no test is shown or modified, it's unclear such a test exists or was run. This is exactly the kind of regression a targeted unit test on log_request/log.py's header formatting should catch: constructing a request with a Referer containing a sensitive query param and asserting it does not appear verbatim in the JSON output.

findings.title: `extra_param_keys` appears to have no remaining consumer
findings.body: `_scrub_uri(value, extra_param_keys)` was the only visible use of `extra_param_keys` in this block. After the change, whatever computes or accepts `extra_param_keys` upstream (a parameter, or a value derived from the handler/config) is dead: it is still built or accepted but never read here. That is a symptom that the sanitisation was dropped rather than intentionally replaced — worth confirming against the function signature, since a public parameter that no longer affects behaviour is a silent contract change for callers that pass it expecting redaction.

findings.title: xlinkhref no longer validated, re-enabling javascript: URIs
findings.body:
Before this change, `xlinkhref` was grouped with `href` and `src` so its value was passed to `isAnchorLinkAllowed(value)`, which is the guard that rejects dangerous URL schemes. After the change `xlinkhref` falls through to whatever the default branch does (presumably allow), so markup such as `<svg><a xlink:href="javascript:alert(1)">` is emitted unvalidated. `xlink:href` is an active navigation/resource attribute in SVG and is equivalent in power to `href`, so it must go through the same check. Restore `|| attribute === 'xlinkhref'` in the condition (and keep any normalisation that maps `xlink:href` to `xlinkhref`), and add a regression test asserting a `javascript:` value in `xlink:href` is stripped.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ xlink:href no longer scheme-validated, re-enabling SVG javascript: XSS

findings.body: The condition that previously caught 'xlinkhref' alongside 'href'/'src' has been removed, silently reopening the XSS-via-SVG-xlink:href vector this code was written to close. No test file is part of this diff, so if this regression is wrong, nothing in the test suite would fail to signal it. A test asserting that an 'xlinkhref' attribute with a javascript: or disallowed URL value is rejected (mirroring however 'href'/'src' are presumably tested) would catch exactly this kind of reversion.

findings.title: Project query parameter no longer validated before use as a path
findings.body:
`projectQueryParameter` comes straight from `query.GetProjectQueryParam()` and, after this change, reaches the rest of `list` with no format check at all. The only remaining guard on line 4 compares it against `parameters.Project` and is skipped entirely when the path parameter is empty (`len(parameters.Project) > 0 &&` short-circuits), so a request that supplies only the query parameter passes through unchecked. Since this value is used to build a filesystem path, values such as `../../etc` or absolute paths are now accepted, which is exactly the traversal the removed `ValidateID` call prevented. Restore the `common.ValidateID(projectQueryParameter)` check inside the `len(projectQueryParameter) > 0` branch, before any comparison or downstream use.

findings.title: No test guards the removed ID validation on project query param
findings.body: The diff removes the `common.ValidateID` check on `projectQueryParameter` before it is used (presumably later as part of a filesystem/storage path). No test file is included in this change, so if any existing test suite covers this `list` function, it likely only exercises valid project names and would not fail when invalid/malicious values (e.g. containing `../`) are passed through. This means the security regression described in the PR title would go undetected by the test suite as it stands.

findings.title: DELETE now maps to "push", so push tokens authorize deletions
findings.body:
The previous switch mapped `http.MethodDelete` to the distinct action `"delete"`; the collapsed condition only excludes GET and HEAD, so DELETE falls into the `push` branch. Any credential or token scoped to `push` on a repository will now pass the access check for DELETE (e.g. manifest/blob deletion), which is a strictly broader grant than before. Anything downstream that consumes `ResourceAction.Action` — policy evaluation, scope parsing, audit records — will also never observe `"delete"` again, so policies that grant `delete` explicitly will stop matching while push-only policies start permitting destructive calls.

Restore the explicit DELETE case:

```go
switch request.Method {
case http.MethodHead, http.MethodGet:
    action = "pull"
case http.MethodDelete:
    action = "delete"
default:
    action = "push"
}
```

Note also that the new condition changes unrecognized methods (OPTIONS, TRACE, …) from `pull` to `push`; that direction is fail-closed, but it is an unintended side effect of the same rewrite.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ DELETE now authorised as "push", so push tokens can delete content

findings.title: No test verifies DELETE maps to 'push' (or catches the regression it fixes)
findings.body: The diff changes DELETE requests from being mapped to a distinct 'delete' action to being folded into 'push'. This is exactly the kind of authorization-mapping change that needs a test asserting request.Method == DELETE produces action == "push", and that GET/HEAD still produce "pull". Without such a test, a future edit could silently revert this mapping (re-introducing the original bug or the inverse) and nothing would fail.

findings.title: Public `location` attribute changes type from str to URL
findings.body:
Previously `self.location` preserved exactly what the caller passed (typically a `str`), while only the `Location` header was normalised via `str(URL(location))`. After this change `self.location` is always a `yarl.URL`.

This is an observable contract change for any existing caller or test doing `exc.location == "/redirect/path"`, `exc.location.startswith(...)`, string formatting/concatenation, or JSON-serialising the attribute. `yarl.URL.__eq__` against a `str` returns False rather than comparing textually, so those comparisons fail silently instead of raising — the failure mode is a wrong branch, not a traceback.

Note that the header value is unaffected (line 9 produces the same string as the old line), so the only behavioural delta is the attribute type. If normalisation of the attribute is genuinely wanted, it should be a separate accessor (e.g. keep `self.location = location` and expose a `location_url` property) rather than repurposing the existing public name.

findings.title: No test verifies self.location is now a URL instance
findings.body: The change flips self.location from being assigned the raw `location` argument to being assigned `URL(location)`, altering its public type/contract. No test in this diff asserts `isinstance(exc.location, URL)` or checks equality against a URL object. If this assignment were reverted or broken again, nothing shown would fail.

findings.title: readany() can return empty bytes before EOF after spurious wakeup
findings.body:
`await self._wait('readany')` returning does not guarantee that `self._buffer` is now non-empty — the waiter can be resolved by any producer-side event (a zero-length `feed_data`, a `_wakeup_waiter` from flow-control/timer paths, or EOF being set concurrently in another task) without data actually landing in the buffer. With the loop, control went back around and awaited again; with the single `if`, control falls straight through to `self._read_nowait(-1)`, which returns `b''` while `self._eof` is still False.

For `StreamReader.readany()` an empty return value is the documented end-of-stream signal, so callers doing `while True: chunk = await resp.content.readany(); if not chunk: break` will silently truncate the body instead of blocking for the rest of it. Restore the `while` so the wait is re-entered until either data is buffered or EOF is observed.

findings.title: No test covers spurious-wakeup / empty-buffer-after-wait behavior
findings.body: The change replaces a `while` loop with a single `if`, meaning that if `_wait('readany')` returns without the buffer being populated (spurious wakeup, or partial fill), the code will proceed directly to `_read_nowait(-1)` and may return empty/incorrect data instead of waiting again. No test in this diff exercises this scenario (waiter woken while buffer still empty and eof still False), so this regression would not be caught by the existing test suite as far as this PR shows.

findings.title: Dropping the None guard makes get_cookie raise on missing cookies
findings.body:
The removed condition `self.request.cookies is not None` was the only thing protecting the membership test. When `request.cookies` is `None` — the state the original fix was written for, e.g. a malformed or unparsable `Cookie` header — `name in self.request.cookies` raises `TypeError: argument of type 'NoneType' is not iterable` instead of returning `default`.

This breaks the documented contract on line 2 ("else default"): every caller that treats a missing cookie as a normal, non-exceptional case (session lookup, XSRF, flash messages) now gets an exception propagating out of the handler and a 500 response rather than `None`. Restore the guard, or guarantee at the request-parsing layer that `cookies` is always a dict (e.g. default to `{}`) before landing this simplification.

findings.title: Removed None guard lets a malformed Cookie header raise TypeError
findings.body:
`get_cookie` now does `name in self.request.cookies` with no check that `self.request.cookies` is non-`None`. If cookie parsing yields `None` for an unparseable/malformed `Cookie` header, this raises `TypeError: argument of type 'NoneType' is not iterable` inside any handler that calls `get_cookie` (including `get_secure_cookie`/XSRF paths that build on it), turning a single attacker-supplied header into a 500 on every such endpoint. The header is fully remote-controlled and unauthenticated, so it is trivially repeatable.

Restore the guard, or make the cookie parser guarantee a dict (`{}` on parse failure) so callers can rely on it — but do not drop the check without that guarantee in place.

findings.title: No regression test for cookies=None crash path
findings.body: This change removes the `self.request.cookies is not None` guard that (per the PR description) was added to fix a crash when the Cookie header is malformed and `request.cookies` ends up None. Without a test that sets request.cookies to None (or simulates a malformed Cookie header) and calls get_cookie, this regression would pass all existing tests silently and reintroduce the crash.

findings.title: update_payment_method mutates object without ownership check
findings.body:
`update_payment_method` takes `pm_id` straight from the request path/args, resolves it with `PaymentMethod.get(pm_id)`, then writes `body["billing_name"]` and persists with `pm.save()` — with no authorisation step between the load and the write. The read handler immediately above (line 6) calls `require_owner(current_user(request), pm)` on exactly the same object, so the control exists and is simply not applied here. The `user = current_user(request)` on line 11 is computed and then never used, which is the tell: authentication happens, authorisation does not.

Any authenticated user can enumerate or guess `pm_id` values and rewrite the billing name on payment methods belonging to other accounts (an IDOR). Add `require_owner(user, pm)` directly after line 12, before any mutation, matching the pattern on line 6.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ update_payment_method mutates the object without require_owner

findings.title: Ownership check removed: bulk_export returns any report by ID
findings.body:
`require_owner(user, report)` was the only per-record authorization gate in `bulk_export`. With the loop deleted, the function fetches every `Report.get(rid)` for caller-supplied `report_ids` and serialises it unconditionally, so any authenticated user can enumerate IDs and read reports belonging to other users. findings.body: The diff removes the per-report require_owner(user, report) check from bulk_export, meaning any authenticated user can now export reports they do not own. No test file is included in this change, and no repository context was retrieved showing an existing test that asserts unauthorized users are blocked from bulk_export. If such a test existed and still passed after this change, the test itself would be the always-passing kind (e.g., only checking export contents, not authorization). findings.body: `Report.get(rid)` is called on unvalidated caller input. Previously `require_owner(user, report)` ran on every element first and would almost certainly reject or raise on a missing record; now a `None` from `Report.get` flows directly into `r.to_dict()` on line 7, producing an `AttributeError` (a 500) instead of a 403/404. findings.title: SQL injection via f-string interpolation in search_customers
Interpolated query breaks on apostrophes and LIKE wildcards
findings.body: `term` and `status` are spliced directly into single-quoted SQL literals. Any ordinary value containing an apostrophe (`O'Brien`, `d'Souza`) terminates the literal and produces a syntax error at execution time, so a legitimate search simply fails. Separately, `%` and `_` inside `term` are interpreted as LIKE wildcards rather than literal characters, so a search for `50%` or `a_b` silently returns the wrong rows. Use a bound parameter as `get_customer` on line 5 already does — e.g. `execute("SELECT * FROM customers WHERE name LIKE %s AND status = %s", (f"%{term}%", status))` — and escape wildcard characters in `term` if literal matching is intended.

findings.title: New search_customers function has no test coverage
findings.body: search_customers is new behavior (constructs SQL via f-string interpolation) but no test file is part of this change. If the query logic were wrong—or if it were fixed to use parameterization and something broke callers—nothing in the repository would fail. Add a test that calls search_customers with representative and adversarial inputs (e.g. containing quotes or SQL metacharacters) and asserts on the resulting query/execute call and/or actual returned rows.

findings.body:
Line 7 patches `notify.transport.deliver` (where the function is defined), but the existing passing test on line 2 patches `notify.sender.deliver` — which is only a valid target if `notify/sender.py` does `from notify.transport import deliver`, binding its own module-level name. Rebinding the attribute on `notify.transport` after that import has no effect on the name `send_with_retry` actually resolves, so the real `deliver` executes: the test may perform real I/O, and `is False` passes or fails for reasons unrelated to the retry logic it claims to cover. findings.title: csv_rows joins values without applying csv_escape
findings.body: `csv_rows` renders each cell as `str(r.get(c, ""))` and joins with commas, with no quoting. A value containing a comma (e.g. `"Smith, Jane"`) produces an extra field and shifts every later column; a value containing `"` produces unparseable output. The module defines `csv_escape` immediately below for exactly this, but nothing calls it. Apply it: `",".join(csv_escape(str(r.get(c, ""))) for c in columns)` (or use the stdlib `csv` module, which also handles embedded newlines).

findings.title: csv_rows emits unescaped field values; csv_escape is unused and misses newlines
findings.body:
`csv_rows` (line 7) concatenates `str(r.get(c, ""))` with commas and never passes the value through `csv_escape` added directly below it. Any row value containing a comma splits into extra columns, and any value containing `\n` or `\r` starts a new record in the output — so a caller who can influence a single field can inject arbitrary additional columns or rows into the exported report, which downstream parsers will read as legitimate data.

Two changes: (1) apply `csv_escape` to each field inside `csv_rows`; (2) extend `csv_escape` to quote on `\n` and `\r` as well as `,` and `"` (per RFC 4180). Using the stdlib `csv` module with a `writer` would handle all of this and is worth preferring over the hand-rolled join. If these reports are opened in a spreadsheet, also consider neutralising leading `=`, `+`, `-`, `@` to avoid formula injection.

findings.title: Retry wraps non-idempotent charge; can double-charge on partial failure
findings.body:
`@retry(attempts=3)` on `charge_card` will re-invoke `charge(card_token, amount_cents)` whenever the first call raises. The failures a retry is meant to absorb (connection reset, read timeout, 502 from a proxy) are precisely the ones where the gateway may have already authorised and captured the charge before the response was lost. Each retry then submits a fresh, distinct charge, so the customer is billed up to three times for one request.

This is unlike `fetch_charge` above it, where `get_charge` is a read and retrying is safe.

Two ways to fix, either is acceptable:
- Pass a caller-supplied idempotency key through to `charge(...)` so the gateway collapses duplicate submissions, and keep the retry.
- Drop the retry here and let the caller decide, or retry only on errors that provably occurred before the request was accepted (e.g. DNS/connect failures), not on timeouts or 5xx responses.

Worth confirming what exception classes `reliability.retry` retries on — if it retries on a bare `Exception`, the exposure is the full set above.

findings.title: Referer header logged unscrubbed, leaking auth tokens into logs
findings.body:
`request.headers["Referer"]` is now written verbatim into the structured log line instead of being passed through `_scrub_uri(value, extra_param_keys)`. Jupyter Server accepts authentication via a `?token=...` query parameter; when a user loads such a URL, every subsequent same-origin request carries that full URL — token included — in its `Referer`. On the code path this helper serves (5xx / request logging), the token is then persisted verbatim to the server log via `log_method(json.dumps(headers, indent=2))` on line 6.

Anyone who can read the server log (operators, log-shipping pipelines, bug-report attachments, CI artifacts, or a low-privileged local account depending on log file permissions) obtains a live credential for the notebook server, which grants arbitrary code execution as the server user. Restore the scrubbing:

```python
value = request.headers[header]
if header == "Referer":
    value = _scrub_uri(value, extra_param_keys)
headers[header] = value
```

The removed `case http.MethodDelete: action = "delete"` arm meant a DELETE request produced a `ResourceAction{Action: "delete"}`, which the authorization layer checks against a distinct delete permission. With the collapsed condition, `http.MethodDelete` falls into the `!= GET && != HEAD` branch and yields `"push"`. findings.body:
Previously `self.location` stored exactly the object the caller passed (normally a `str`); only the header got the `str(URL(...))` normalisation. After this change `self.location` is a `yarl.URL`.

Consequences for existing callers and subclasses:

- String operations break at runtime: `exc.location.startswith("/")`, `exc.location + "?x=1"`, `os.path`/`urllib` helpers and `re` matching on it all raise `AttributeError`/`TypeError`.
- Comparisons fail *silently*: `yarl.URL("/foo") == "/foo"` is `False`, so tests and middleware that assert `exc.location == "/login"` start taking the wrong branch rather than erroring loudly.
- `URL()` percent-encodes/normalises, so even `str(exc.location)` is not guaranteed to round-trip to what was passed in.

If the intent is only to avoid constructing `URL` twice, keep the attribute's observable type stable, e.g. build a local `url = URL(location)` for the header and leave `self.location = location`; if the URL form really is wanted, expose it under a new name (or a property) and note the change as a breaking API change.

findings.title: readany can return b'' without EOF after a spurious wakeup
findings.body:
`_wait('readany')` returning does not guarantee that data arrived — the waiter is resolved by any event that wakes the reader (feed_data with an empty payload, feed_eof, exception set, flow-control/resume wakeups). The `while` loop re-checked `self._buffer`/`self._eof` after waking and went back to waiting if neither held. With a plain `if`, a single wakeup that produced no data falls straight through to `return self._read_nowait(-1)`, which yields `b''` while the stream is neither at EOF nor in an error state.

That breaks the documented contract of this coroutine: consumers (e.g. `async for chunk in resp.content.iter_any()` / `iter_chunked` style loops, and anything that uses `if not chunk: break`) treat empty bytes as end-of-stream, so the body is silently truncated instead of the read blocking until real data or EOF. Restore the loop:

```python
while not self._buffer and not self._eof:
    await self._wait('readany')
```

No test in this diff exercises repeated/looped waiting behavior on `_wait('readany')`, so this regression would not be caught by any existing or added test.

findings.title: search_customers interpolates term/status directly into SQL
findings.body:
`term` and `status` are spliced into the SQL text with an f-string and the statement is executed with no parameters. Two concrete consequences:

1. Any caller-supplied value containing a single quote (a name like `O'Brien`, or a crafted `status` of `x' OR '1'='1`) terminates the literal early — at best a syntax error at runtime, at worst arbitrary predicate or statement injection.
2. `%` and `_` inside `term` are LIKE metacharacters and are not escaped, so a term containing them silently matches the wrong rows.

Use the same parameterised form as `get_customer` on line 5, moving the wildcards into the bound value:

```python
def search_customers(term, status):
    sql = "SELECT * FROM customers WHERE name LIKE %s AND status = %s"
    return execute(sql, (f"%{term}%", status))
```

If LIKE metacharacters in `term` must be treated literally, escape them explicitly and add an `ESCAPE` clause.

findings.title: csv_rows never applies csv_escape, emitting malformed CSV
findings.body: `csv_rows` joins stringified cell values with `","` directly. Any value containing a comma, a double quote, or a newline will break the record: a single field with a comma silently becomes two columns, and downstream parsers will either error or misalign every subsequent column. The fix is already in the same file \u2014 route each cell through `csv_escape`, e.g. `",".join(csv_escape(str(r.get(c, ""))) for c in columns)`. Note also that `csv_escape` assumes a `str` (it uses `in` on `value`), so the `str(...)` conversion must happen before the escape call, and RFC4180 also requires quoting values containing `\n`/`\r`, which the current predicate on line 12 does not cover.

Any value containing a comma, a double quote, or a newline injects extra fields or extra records into the rendered CSV, meaning the row data — not the caller — controls the document structure. Where those rows originate from user-supplied content (report names, free-text fields), this is a data-controlled format injection, and consumers that open the file in a spreadsheet are additionally exposed to formula injection via values beginning with `=`, `+`, `-` or `@`.

Suggested fix: apply `csv_escape` inside the comprehension, extend `csv_escape` to also quote values containing `\n` or `\r`, coerce to `str` before the membership tests (today `csv_escape(1)` raises `TypeError`), and consider prefixing leading `=+-@` with `'` if the output is intended for spreadsheets. The stdlib `csv` module handles all of this correctly and is usually the better answer.

findings.title: Retry wraps a non-idempotent charge, risking duplicate charges
findings.body:
`charge(card_token, amount_cents)` is a state-mutating payment operation. `@retry(attempts=3)` will re-invoke it on any failure the decorator considers retryable, including a network timeout or 5xx that occurs *after* the gateway has already accepted and captured the charge. The result is up to three real charges against the customer's card for one logical request.

The read wrapper directly above (`fetch_charge` -> `get_charge`) is safe precisely because it is idempotent; the same decorator is not transferable to the write path.

Fixes, in rough order of preference:
- Pass a caller-supplied idempotency key through to `charge(...)` so the gateway collapses retried attempts into one charge, and only then retry.
- If the gateway has no idempotency support, drop the retry here and surface the failure, or retry only on errors that provably occurred before submission (e.g. connection-refused / DNS), never on timeouts or 5xx.

This is a critical contract gap for a financial operation.

On a table large enough to warrant a composite `(tenant_id, created_at DESC)` index, that is a write outage for the length of the build.

Use `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY`, noting that it cannot run inside a transaction block — so the migration runner must be configured to execute this statement outside its usual wrapping transaction, and the migration should be checked for a left-behind `INVALID` index on failure.

findings.title: readany can return empty bytes before EOF after while→if change
findings.body:
`_wait('readany')` returning does not guarantee that `self._buffer` is now non-empty. The waiter future is resolved by any of the wake-up paths (e.g. `feed_data` with a zero-length payload, `feed_eof`, `set_exception`, or a cancellation/timeout-adjacent wake), so control can reach `self._read_nowait(-1)` with an empty buffer and no EOF set. `_read_nowait(-1)` then returns `b''`.

That breaks the documented contract of `readany`: it must return a non-empty chunk unless the stream is at EOF. Every consumer that loops `while True: chunk = await content.readany(); if not chunk: break` — including `__aiter__`/`iter_any` style iteration — will silently treat the empty result as end-of-stream and truncate the response body. No exception is raised, so the failure is a silent short read.

Restore the loop so the wake-up condition is re-checked:

```python
while not self._buffer and not self._eof:
    await self._wait('readany')
```

The loop form is the standard guard against spurious wakeups and is what the original fix introduced; the `if` form is strictly weaker and only coincidentally correct when the wake always carries data.


findings.title: csv_rows joins raw values and never calls csv_escape
findings.body:
`csv_rows` joins `str(r.get(c, ""))` with commas directly. Any cell containing a comma, a double quote, or a newline is emitted unescaped, producing a line with the wrong field count that no CSV reader will parse back correctly. `csv_escape`, added immediately below in the same commit, is exactly the fix and is currently unreferenced (dead code) — the row builder should be `",".join(csv_escape(str(r.get(c, ""))) for c in columns)`.

Note also that `csv_escape` assumes a `str`: `"," in value` raises `TypeError` for an int, float or `None`. Wiring it in after the `str(...)` conversion in `csv_rows` avoids that, but any other caller passing a raw cell value will hit it.

findings.title: csv_rows joins fields unescaped, bypassing csv_escape
findings.body:
`csv_rows` renders each field with `str(r.get(c, ""))` and joins on `,`, never calling the `csv_escape` helper defined immediately below it. Any field value that contains a comma (or a quote, or a newline) will split into additional CSV fields, shifting every subsequent column for that row and letting whoever controls the field content forge column values in the exported file. If the row data originates from user-supplied records, this is field-delimiter injection into the export consumed downstream (spreadsheet import, billing pipeline, etc.).

Fix: apply the escaping on the way out, e.g. `",".join(csv_escape(str(r.get(c, ""))) for c in columns)`, and extend `csv_escape` to also quote values containing `\n`/`\r`. Using `csv.writer` from the stdlib would remove the whole class of bug. Separately, consider whether values beginning with `=`, `+`, `-` or `@` need neutralising for spreadsheet formula injection.

findings.title: New exporter functions added with no tests
findings.body: csv_rows, csv_escape (this file), dump_streaming, dump_pretty (json_export.py), and margins_for, usable_width (pdf_export.py) are all new public functions with non-trivial logic (chunking, escaping rules, margin arithmetic) but no test file is included in the diff. A bug in escaping logic (e.g. missing check for both comma and embedded quote combos), an off-by-one in chunk_size slicing, or wrong margin math would go undetected. Recommend adding unit tests covering: csv_escape with commas/quotes, csv_rows with mixed columns, dump_streaming boundary chunk sizes, dump_pretty key ordering, and margins_for/usable_width for known page sizes.
